title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 227
paragraphs: As for Egypt, I both believe those who say these things are so, and I am strongly of that opinion myself. I have observed that Egypt projects into the sea further than the adjoining land; that shells are found on its mountains; that an efflorescence of salt forms upon the surface, so that even the pyramids are being eaten away by it; and that of all the mountains of Egypt, only the range above Memphis has sand. Besides which, I notice that Egypt resembles neither Arabia which borders upon it, nor Libya, nor yet Syria (for Syrians are the ones who dwell along the Arabian seacoast), but has a black and easily crumbling soil — which is in truth mud and silt brought down from Ethiopia by the river. The soil of Libya, as we know, is reddish in colour and rather sandy, while that of Arabia and Syria is clayey and rocky.
